For left main disease, randomized trials demonstrate broadly comparable mid-term outcomes between CABG and PCI. However, PCI is associated with higher rates of repeat revascularization and, in some analyses, higher late death/MI, especially in people with diabetes with high SYNTAX scores [ 38 , 39 , 40 ]. Both guidelines support the physiological assessment of non-culprit stenoses to guide revascularization (ACC/AHA Class 2b; ESC Class 2b) and mandate a multidisciplinary Heart Team approach that integrates coronary anatomy, left ventricular function, diabetes, frailty, stroke risk, and patient preference. In older or frail patients, viability testing, overall comorbidity burden, and goals of care often limit surgical plans. In such cases, culprit-only PCI, staged PCI, or hybrid strategies (culprit PCI initially, followed by CABG) remain reasonable options when clinical stability permits [ 39 , 40 ].

4.4 Complete vs. Culprit-Only Revascularization in NSTEMI With PCI For STEMI, several large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) (PRAMI, DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI, COMPLETE) support complete revascularization of suitable non-culprit lesions, usually in a staged fashion, thereby reducing reinfarction and repeat revascularization [ 40 , 41 , 42 ]. However, in Type 1 NSTEMI, there is no large, dedicated randomized clinical trial definitively establishing a complete-versus-culprit PCI strategy. While CABG typically achieves complete revascularization, evidence for complete revascularization with PCI is based on smaller trials and observational/meta-analytic data. The SMILE trial, a small, two-center study, suggested that complete revascularization (often staged) reduces the need for repeat ischemia/revascularization without clear safety penalties. In the SMILE trial (584 patients, two-center, unblinded), single-stage complete revascularization reduced the 1-year composite major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) endpoint by approximately 45% compared with multistage PCI (13.6% vs. 23.2%), driven primarily by a 48% relative reduction in target vessel revascularization (8.3% vs. 15.2%). No significant differences were observed in the individual hard endpoints of death or reinfarction [ 43 ].

Additional data supporting complete revascularization were identified from FAMOUS-NSTEMI, a physiology-guided NSTEMI strategy, which showed that fractional flow reserve (FFR) can safely defer non-ischemic lesions and reduce stent use without worsening outcomes, implying that “functionally complete” rather than purely angiographically complete revascularization may be optimal [ 44 ]. Contemporary meta-analyses and registries generally favor treating significant non-culprit disease, either during the index procedure or staged, when lesion severity is supported by physiology or clear ischemia, with approximately 27–47% relative reductions in composite MACEs compared with culprit-only PCI [ 45 ]. Accordingly, the 2025 ACS guidelines provide a Class 1 recommendation in stable patients with NSTE-ACS and multivessel disease (MVD), without left main stenosis, who are not intended for CABG and who undergo culprit-lesion PCI: PCI of significant non-culprit lesions (at the time of the index procedure or as a staged procedure) is recommended to reduce the risk of MACEs [ 29 ].

Who benefits most from complete PCI? Younger patients with few comorbidities, clear multivessel ischemia, and complex culprit biology ( e . g ., large plaque burden) tend to benefit from a planned, staged, complete approach. Who might not? Older, frail patients or those with severe CKD, anemia, high bleeding risk, or tortuous/diffuse small-vessel disease may be better served with culprit-only PCI plus optimal medical therapy, reserving non-culprit revascularization for refractory symptoms or objective ischemia (opinion-based). In practice, a Heart Team-based, physiology-guided, staged strategy is most consistent with current guidance while we await a definitive NSTEMI-specific RCT [ 29 , 30 , 31 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 ].

When PCI is pursued in the NSTEMI setting, particularly for complex or multivessel disease, contemporary evidence increasingly supports the use of intravascular imaging (IVUS or OCT) to guide procedural decision-making [ 46 ]. This is a Class 1 recommendation in the 2025 ACS guidelines. Intravascular imaging can optimize stent sizing, characterize plaque morphology and composition, confirm adequate stent expansion and apposition, and detect complications such as edge dissection or tissue protrusion that may not be apparent on angiography alone. These modalities are particularly valuable in NSTEMI, where culprit lesion identification may be challenging, and in cases of suspected SCAD, when OCT is used selectively to distinguish dissection flaps from atherosclerotic disease [ 46 ].

5. Conclusion NSTEMI is a heterogeneous clinical syndrome that encompasses a spectrum of mechanisms, including atherothrombotic plaque disruption (rupture, erosion, and calcified nodules), dynamic epicardial or microvascular obstruction, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, thromboembolism, and supply–demand imbalance; each mechanism has distinct diagnostic pathways and therapeutic implications. Moving from a broad syndromic label to a personalized mechanism-specific diagnosis is imperative. In selected cases, standard evaluation may be insufficient, and more advanced diagnostic tools, if available, may be needed, as described in patients with MINOCA. However, in the vast majority of cases, good clinical judgment, along with standard diagnostic and therapeutic tools, should be sufficient to establish an appropriate diagnosis and guide effective treatment.

6. Future Developments For atherosclerotic disease and Type 1 MI, prevention is essential. Earlier detection and treatment of atherosclerosis are critical to significantly reduce Type 1 MI (both STEMI and NSTEMI). Clinicians should aim to identify at-risk patients earlier in the disease course through appropriate screening and risk-factor modification. Potential approaches include coronary artery calcium scoring and, ideally, CT angiography or other techniques in appropriately selected high-risk patients. CT angiography can identify asymptomatic plaque burden and plaque characteristics, particularly low-attenuation plaque. In the multicenter SCOT-HEART trial, low-attenuation noncalcified plaque burden on CCTA emerged as the strongest independent predictor of future fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction, outperforming cardiovascular risk scores, coronary artery calcium scoring, and stenosis severity. Patients with low-attenuation plaque burden exceeding 4% had an almost 5-fold increased risk of subsequent MI [ 47 , 48 , 49 ]. A recent expert consensus statement from the Quantitative Cardiovascular Imaging Study Group provided evidence-based recommendations for integrating CCTA with artificial intelligence (AI)-supported plaque analysis to individualize treatment based on atherosclerotic plaque characterization, highlighting low-attenuation plaque and positive remodeling as key features for cardiovascular risk assessment [ 50 ].

Lifelong attention to modifiable risk factors, including hypertension, diet/exercise/obesity, low-density lipoprotein levels, avoidance of smoking/other pollutants, and glucose control (HbA1c) in patients with diabetes, is essential and should be a priority for anyone who values optimal cardiovascular health. Patients with a family history of premature myocardial infarction, stroke, or sudden death in adulthood should also have lipoprotein(a) measured. Recent guidelines recommend screening for atherosclerosis beginning at age 30 years, using the PREVENT Risk Calculator (refer clinicians to contemporary lipid and hypertension guidelines for additional recommendations) [ 51 ].

6.1 Artificial Intelligence in Diagnosis and Management AI holds considerable promise for earlier detection, more precise risk stratification, and improved imaging interpretation; however, AI also requires prospective validation, equitable performance across populations, and smooth integration into clinical workflows [ 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 ]. Potential applications include automated interpretation of symptoms and ECGs, serial biomarker testing to enable earlier diagnosis or safe early discharge, and AI-based plaque characterization using intravascular or noninvasive imaging [ 56 , 57 ]. Barriers to widespread clinical adoption include the need for robust external validation across diverse populations, integration into existing care pathways, clinician interpretability, and the risk of bias. Current guidelines acknowledge the promise of AI but stop short of recommending routine adoption. Ongoing prospective studies will determine whether AI improves actionable outcomes, including time to therapy, bleeding-adjusted net clinical benefit, and resource utilization [ 51 ].

6.2 Unanswered Questions 6.2.1 Plaque Erosion: A Distinct Mechanism Requiring Tailored Management Unlike plaque rupture, which involves disruption of a thin fibrous cap overlying a macrophage-infiltrated, lipid-rich necrotic core, plaque erosion is characterized by endothelial denudation over a proteoglycan- and smooth muscle cell-rich plaque without cap disruption. Moreover, plaque erosion is driven by innate immune mechanisms, including Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) activation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and hyaluronan degradation, and results in a predominantly platelet-rich (white), nonocclusive thrombus [ 58 , 59 ]. Erosion accounts for approximately 25–40% of ACS cases in younger patients, women, and smokers with fewer traditional risk factors, and represents a majority of coronary thrombi in women under 50 years of age [ 60 ]. Currently, in addition to a healthy lifestyle, there is no consensus on strategies to prevent plaque erosion. Further studies are required.

6.2.2 Invasive Strategy in Type 2 NSTEMI Type 2 NSTEMI is associated with higher in-hospital and post-discharge mortality than Type 1 NSTEMI [ 14 ]. While patients with Type 2 NSTEMI have more comorbidities, current data do not establish CAD as the cause of the higher mortality. However, CAD is often present among patients undergoing invasive evaluation. These patients are routinely excluded from ACS intervention trials, leaving no randomized evidence to guide whether, when, or in whom angiography and/or revascularization should be performed. Observational data suggest that a subset of patients with underlying obstructive CAD may benefit from invasive evaluation once the inciting trigger is corrected, but reliably identifying this subgroup remains challenging [ 30 ]. Prospective trials are needed to determine which Type 2 NSTEMI patients warrant coronary angiography or revascularization, and to define the optimal timing relative to the precipitating condition.

6.2.3 Prasugrel Versus Ticagrelor Both prasugrel and ticagrelor are preferred over clopidogrel in ACS patients undergoing PCI, yet guidelines diverge in their recommendations. The 2023 ESC guidelines assign prasugrel a Class 2a preference based primarily on the open-label ISAR-REACT 5 trial, whereas the 2025 ACC/AHA guidelines consider prasugrel and ticagrelor interchangeable (Class 1), citing design limitations that constrain the generalizability of a single study [ 29 , 31 , 61 , 62 , 63 ]. Prasugrel remains contraindicated in patients with prior stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA) and requires dose reduction in older or low-weight patients. In contrast, ticagrelor is the only potent P2Y12 inhibitor with Class 1 guideline support for medically managed NSTE-ACS without planned PCI [ 29 , 63 ]. A definitive double-anonymized head-to-head trial is still needed.

6.2.4 DAPT After Drug-Coated Balloon (DCB) Angioplasty DCBs deliver drugs without leaving a permanent scaffold. Trials such as BASKET-SMALL 2 and DEBUT support their efficacy in small-vessel disease and in patients at HBR [ 64 , 65 , 66 , 67 ]. One randomized trial demonstrated the non-inferiority of stepwise DAPT de-escalation compared with standard 12-month DAPT in ACS patients treated exclusively with DCB [ 68 ]. The International DCB Consensus Group endorses only 4 weeks of DAPT after DCB-only angioplasty. Nevertheless, current ESC guidelines still extrapolate longer DAPT durations from stent-based data, underscoring the need for larger confirmatory trials [ 31 , 64 ].

6.2.5 Updated Nomenclature for STEMI/NSTEMI? Over the years, the nomenclature for what one now refers to as NSTEMI has evolved. As outlined in the historical perspective, the original terminology was non-transmural MI. It then changed over time to subendocardial or non-Q-wave MI and finally NSTEMI. New data suggests that further evolution should be considered. It has been shown that NSTEMI with total coronary occlusion of the infarct-related artery has a worse prognosis than NSTEMI without total occlusion but similar to STEMI with total occlusion [ 69 ]. Thus, nomenclature should now reflect the presence of total occlusion as it provides a more accurate classification of STEMI/NSTEMI. However, the authors of this review do not necessarily concur that new terminology is required as in a large percentage of NSTEMI, one is unable to assign an infarct-related artery.

Antiplatelet pretreatment in patients with non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) is controversial. It is vital that the risk of ischaemia and the risk of haemorrhage are both considered when managing this patient group. Current clinical guidelines do not recommend routine pretreatment in patients presenting with NSTE-ACS who are having coronary angiography within 24 hours. However, a significant portion of these patients will not have coronary angiography until after 24 hours. Pretreatment with antiplatelets may reduce the risk of ischaemic events, but it is associated with bleeding and delays to coronary artery bypass grafting, and it may be deleterious in patients with diagnoses other than NSTE-ACS, such as acute aortic syndromes, pulmonary embolism or intracranial bleeds. This review analyses the most important studies assessing antiplatelet pretreatment in NSTE-ACS.

Keywords Pretreatment bleeding misdiagnosis surgery delay coronary angiography pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement no pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) are usually caused by the rupture of a vulnerable plaque that leads to the activation of platelets and a coagulation cascade, resulting in thrombus formation with consequent compromised coronary blood flow that causes myocardial ischaemia or necrosis. Current evidence recommends dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and a potent P2Y 12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel) as the standard therapy for non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) patients, while clopidogrel should be reserved for patients with a high bleeding risk, contraindications for high intensity DAPT or for those with an indication for oral anticoagulation. 1 , 2

A key consideration in the management of antithrombotic therapy in patients with NSTE-ACS is the balance between ischaemic events and bleeding events. Ischaemic events comprise spontaneous MI and device-related MI as defined in the universal definition of MI. 3 Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)-related MI (type 4a MI) requires an elevation of cardiac troponin (cTn) values more than five times the 99th percentile upper range limit (URL) in patients with normal baseline values or an increase of >20% in patients with elevated cTn before the procedure to an absolute value more than five times the 99th percentile URL with evidence of new myocardial ischaemia, such as ECG changes, imaging evidence or from procedure-related complications. Another subcategory of PCI-related MI is stent/scaffold thrombosis (type 4b MI), as documented by angiography or autopsy using the same criteria as type 1 MI. 3

Multiple definitions have been used for bleeding in clinical trials and registries; however, they generally include non-coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)-related bleeding (classified as major, minor or minimal), as well as bleeding in the setting of CABG. Among the most commonly used classifications in these studies are the Thrombolysis in MI (TIMI) grading system, the Bleeding Academic Research Consortium criteria, and the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis criteria. 4

Ischaemic events and bleeding events have a similar prognostic impact; therefore, a comprehensive approach that considers ischaemic and bleeding risk is essential for the management of antiplatelet therapy in patients with NSTE-ACS. 5

Pretreatment is defined as the administration of a P2Y 12 inhibitor before an invasive coronary angiogram (CAG) is performed. 6 It has been associated with increased bleeding events without ischaemic benefit in patients in whom CAG is performed within the first 24 hours of presentation with ACS, and it may be deleterious in patients with misdiagnoses who have acute aortic syndromes, pulmonary embolisms or intracranial bleedings. 7 , 8 Moreover, pretreatment may also delay surgical treatment in patients who require CABG. For these reasons, current guidelines do not recommend routine pretreatment in NSTE-ACS patients when an early invasive strategy is feasible. However, these recommendations are based on the results of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in which the mean time to CAG is extremely short (2–4 hours), so they do not allow time for a hypothetical benefit of pretreatment and are often not representative of routine clinical practice for these patients, where delays to CAG are longer, especially if the NSTE-ACS occurs during weekends or holidays or in centres where access to the cath lab is not available 24/7, 365 days a year. 7 , 8 Clinicians must decide whether or not to administer pretreatment to NSTE-ACS patients. It is unclear if pretreatment has the same effects across the entire spectrum of NSTE-ACS, such as with non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI) and unstable angina (UA) patients. 9

The present focused narrative review evaluates the most relevant clinical trials assessing the safety and efficacy of pretreatment in NSTE-ACS patients. Aiming to compare current evidence with our experience, our clinical research group also performed an observational study assessing pretreatment-related outcomes in a cohort of NSTE-ACS patients, in a centre without 24/7 access to a cath lab or access to a local cardiac surgery team. We also devised an algorithm that aims to help clinicians select which patients may benefit from antiplatelet pretreatment.

Methods This article includes a narrative review of the available evidence on antiplatelet pretreatment in NSTE-ACS. A structured, non-systematic literature search was performed using PubMed, including studies published up to 2026. Search terms included combinations of “NSTE-ACS”, “pretreatment”, “P2Y 12 inhibitors”, “ticagrelor”, “prasugrel” and “clopidogrel”. We prioritised RCTs, meta-analyses and guideline documents and complemented this evidence with selected observational studies reflecting real-world clinical practice. Studies were selected based on their clinical relevance to the timing of antiplatelet therapy and associated ischaemic and bleeding outcomes.

Dual Antiplatelet Therapy in NSTE-ACS The interpretation of available evidence on antiplatelet pretreatment in NSTE-ACS requires several interrelated but conceptually different factors to be distinguished: the pretreatment strategy, referring to the timing of P2Y12 inhibitor administration relative to CAG; the choice of P2Y12 inhibitor, with different pharmacodynamic profiles; the timing to CAG, which determines the potential window for drug efficacy; and the clinical and procedural context, including differences between earlier PCI-era practices and contemporary management characterised by radial access and early invasive strategies. Failure to differentiate between these aspects may contribute to the heterogeneity of results across clinical trials.

The recommendation for DAPT with aspirin and clopidogrel in patients with ACS was established in the 2002 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of ACS in patients presenting without persistent ST-segment elevation, after the publication of the COMMIT and PCI CURE studies, which showed a reduction in ischaemic and cardiovascular events in these patients, with no significant excess risk of bleeding. 10 , 11 Other studies showed a significant increase in bleeding events among patients treated with DAPT. 12

However, several studies showed that clopidogrel exhibits variable and dose-dependent platelet inhibition with a maximum inhibitory response to the 300 mg clopidogrel loading dose within 24 hours, with resistance (described as <10% reduction in aggregation in response to 5 μmol/l adenosine diphosphate), and poor response to clopidogrel antiplatelet activity in about 30% of patients, with an associated with a higher risk of stent thrombosis and recurrent ischaemic events. 13 – 16 This concern about clopidogrel resistance led to an investigation of alternative pharmacological strategies with a more effective antiplatelet effect and faster onset of action.

In 2007, the TRITON-TIMI 38 trial compared prasugrel with clopidogrel in 13,608 ACS patients scheduled to undergo PCI. 2 The primary efficacy endpoint – a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI or non-fatal stroke – occurred in 12.1% versus 9.9% in the clopidogrel and prasugrel groups, respectively (HR 0.81; 95% CI [0.73–0.90]; p<0.001). Significant reductions in the rates of MI, urgent target vessel revascularisation and stent thrombosis were observed in the prasugrel group. The key safety endpoint of major bleeding was also observed more frequently in the prasugrel group (2.4% versus 1.8%; HR 1.32; 95% CI [1.03–1.68]; p=0.03).

In 2009, the PLATO trial randomised 18,624 ACS patients to receive ticagrelor (37.5% STEMI patients) or clopidogrel (38% STEMI patients). 1 The primary endpoint (cardiovascular mortality, MI or stroke) occurred less frequently in the ticagrelor group (9.8% versus 11.7%; HR 0.84; 95% CI [0.77–0.92]; p<0.001). The rate of stent thrombosis was lower in the ticagrelor group (1.3% versus 1.9%; p=0.009). The benefit of ticagrelor was also observed for the individual components of MI and cardiovascular death, but not for stroke. No significant difference was found in the rates of major bleeding, but ticagrelor was associated with a higher rate of major bleeding not related to CABG (4.5% versus 3.8%; p=0.03) and more episodes of intracranial bleeding (0.3% versus 0.2%; p=0.06).

The results of these clinical trials led to the recommendation of DAPT using a potent P2Y 12 inhibitor, such as ticagrelor or prasugrel, as the standard therapy for patients with NSTE-ACS, while clopidogrel should be reserved for patients with a high bleeding risk, such as older patients or those with chronic kidney disease or previous bleedings, contraindications for high intensity DAPT (e.g prasugrel is not recommended in patients ≥75 years, ≤60 kg or with a history of cerebrovascular accident) or in those with an indication for oral anticoagulation. 1 , 2 As both ischaemic and major bleeding events have a similar prognostic impact in these patients, an integral approach considering not only ischaemic risk, but also haemorrhagic risk is a key point for the management of NSTE-ACS patients. 5

The Academic Research Consortium for High Bleeding Risk criteria are a useful tool to identify high-risk patients who may require DAPT tapering. 17 To minimise the risk of bleeding associated with DAPT in patients with ACS, a second antiplatelet agent (prasugrel, ticagrelor or clopidogrel) must be chosen and a decision made on the best time to administer it. The need for pretreatment across the spectrum of ACS has subsequently been questioned. There are severe clinical conditions, such as acute aortic syndromes, pulmonary embolism or stroke, which can be misdiagnosed as an ACS, and the use of DAPT can be deleterious in these cases. For this reason, it is recommended that pretreatment in the prehospital setting is avoided in favour of waiting for a more cautious evaluation and the results of complementary tests, such as blood tests, chest X-ray and echocardiogram, to consider alternative diagnoses.

Perioperative bleeding and surgical delay are major concerns in ACS patients treated with DAPT when CABG is required. In 2025, the RAPID CABG randomised open-label non-inferiority trial enrolled 143 ACS patients and compared early CABG surgery 2–3 days after ticagrelor cessation versus delaying surgery to 5–7 days and found that an early surgical strategy was non-inferior in incurring perioperative bleeding. 18 Moreover, it was observed that a reduction in the delay between ticagrelor cessation and CABG surgery may decrease the length of hospital stay.

Despite the benefit of DAPT at the time of PCI in reducing ischaemic events, the net clinical benefit is doubtful when the bleeding risk, the delay to surgery and the use of DAPT in patients with a final diagnosis different to ACS are considered. For these reasons, several trials have evaluated the safety and efficacy of pretreatment in NSTE-ACS. 7 , 8 , 18 – 21

Comparative RCTs Assessing Antiplatelet Pretreatment for NSTE-ACS In the PCI CURE study, 2,658 patients with NSTE-ACS undergoing PCI were randomised to receive pretreatment with a loading dose of 300 mg clopidogrel or placebo. 11 The number of patients with the primary endpoint of cardiovascular death, MI or urgent revascularisation was significantly lower in the clopidogrel group than in the placebo group (7.2%; n=73 versus 4.2%; n=41, RR 0.58; 95% CI [0.40–0.85]; p=0.005). This reduction in the primary endpoint was seen from the second day after PCI and maintained until 30 days and after 8 months of follow-up. This benefit of clopidogrel pretreatment was seen in the subgroup of patients who had PCI >72 hours after randomisation, while there were no statistically significant differences in those who had CAG <72 hours after randomisation.

Most patients were treated with a thienopyridine after PCI (>80% in both groups), suggesting that this early postprocedural benefit was due to pretreatment with clopidogrel. There were no significant differences in major bleeding between groups, while minor bleeds were more frequent in the clopidogrel group than the placebo group at the end of follow-up.

The CREDO trial assessed the benefit of pretreatment with a clopidogrel 300 mg loading dose plus aspirin 3–24 hours before PCI. 19 Participants had low ischaemic risk (32.8% with stable angina, approximately 53% with UA, and approximately 13–14% with recent MI) and were randomly assigned to clopidogrel (n=1,053) or placebo (n=1,063). After PCI, all patients received 75 mg clopidogrel until day 28. From day 29 to 12 months, patients in the loading dose group received 75 mg clopidogrel and those in the control group received a placebo. Pretreatment with clopidogrel did not reduce ischaemic events in the overall cohort. However, in a prespecified subgroup analysis, patients who received clopidogrel ≥6 hours before PCI presented a relative risk reduction of 38.6% (95% CI [-1.6, 62.9]; p=0.051) in the combined risk of death, MI or urgent target vessel revascularisation at 28 days. No significant differences were found in bleeding events.

The ARMYDA-5 PRELOAD trial did not find statistically significant differences in a 600 mg clopidogrel loading dose 4–8 hours before PCI or a 600 mg loading dose given in the cath lab after CAG, but prior to PCI. 20 No differences were found in either ischaemic events or bleeding events between groups. Nevertheless, the study had a small cohort (n=409), and only 40% of participants had ACS (UA or NSTE-ACS).

In 2013, the ACCOAST trial enrolled 4,033 patients with NSTE-ACS and randomised patients to receive pretreatment with prasugrel 30 mg or placebo. 8 When PCI was indicated, an additional 30 mg of prasugrel was administered in the pretreatment group, while 60 mg of prasugrel was given in the control group. The TIMI major bleeding rate was increased in the pretreatment group (HR 1.9; 95% CI [1.19–3.02]; p=0.006), but no significant differences were observed in the primary efficacy endpoint (a composite of cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, urgent revascularisation or glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor bailout up to day 7). It is important to note that femoral access was above 50% and the time from loading dose to CAG was 4.4 hours and 4.2 hours in the pretreatment and the no pretreatment group, respectively.

In 2019, the ISAR-REACT 5 trial compared ticagrelor with prasugrel in 4,108 patients presenting with ACS (59% NSTE-ACS and 41% STEMI). 7 In the ticagrelor group, the loading dose was administered as soon as possible, while in the prasugrel group, the timing of the loading dose was dependent on the clinical presentation. In NSTE-ACS patients, the loading dose was postponed until the patient’s coronary anatomy was known but before PCI, while in STEMI patients, 60 mg of prasugrel was administered as soon as possible. The primary endpoint was the composite of death, MI or stroke at 1-year follow-up, and it was observed in 9.3% and 6.9% of the ticagrelor and prasugrel groups, respectively (HR 1.36; 95% CI [1.09–1.70]; p=0.006). The safety endpoint was bleeding events, and no significantly differences were found between groups.

In 2020, the DUBIUS trial randomised 1,449 NSTE-ACS patients (approximately 20% UA and 80% NSTEMI) to receive pretreatment with ticagrelor or no pretreatment. 21 Both strategies were associated with a low incidence of ischaemic events and bleeding events, suggesting that one strategy was unlikely to be more effective than the other, leading to premature discontinuation of the study. No differences were also found depending on whether the CAG was performed within the first 24 hours or later after enrolment.

The differing results across trials can be explained by three key factors: timing to CAG, pharmacodynamic profiles of P2Y12 inhibitors and changes in contemporary practice. Early trials, such as PCI-CURE and CREDO, were conducted in an era of longer delays to CAG (>24 hours), where upstream pretreatment allowed sufficient time for clopidogrel, which is characterised by relatively slow and variable platelet inhibition, to achieve therapeutic effect before PCI. 11 , 19 In contrast, more recent studies (ACCOAST, ISAR-REACT 5 and DUBIUS) reflect a paradigm of early invasive management (often within 2–4 hours) in which the pharmacodynamic profile of oral P2Y12 inhibitors may be mismatched with the short interval to PCI. 7 , 8 , 21 This temporal mismatch is particularly relevant for prasugrel and ticagrelor, whose onset of action, although faster than clopidogrel, may still be insufficient when CAG is performed very early, thereby attenuating any ischaemic benefit of pretreatment while exposing patients to an increased bleeding risk.

Contemporary practice has evolved substantially. Radial access was used in a minority of patients in ACCOAST (approximately 40–45%), compared with a substantially higher adoption in ISAR-REACT 5 (approximately 80– 85%) and DUBIUS (>85%), whereas earlier trials, such as PCI-CURE and CREDO, were conducted predominantly with femoral access. 7 , 8 , 11 , 19 , 21 This progressive shift toward radial access has reduced the bleeding risk associated with pretreatment strategies. Likewise, anticoagulation strategies have shifted from routine use of unfractionated heparin frequently combined with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in earlier trials, toward more contemporary approaches including weight-adjusted unfractionated heparin or bivalirudin, with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors largely reserved for bailout situations. Additional sources of heterogeneity include differences in study populations (for example, NSTEMI-only versus mixed cohorts), timing of randomisation, crossover rates and the proportion of patients ultimately undergoing PCI. Overall, the benefit-risk balance of P2Y 12 inhibitor pretreatment appears highly dependent on context, with potential benefits in delayed invasive strategies. Based on this evidence, current clinical guidelines do not recommend routine administration of pretreatment in patients with NSTE-ACS for whom early CAG (<24 hours) is planned.

Gaps in Evidence In daily clinical practice, a substantial proportion of patients with NSTE-ACS are treated in hospitals that do not have 24/7 access to a cath lab. This subgroup remains underrepresented in large RCTs from which current pretreatment recommendations are derived, resulting in a relative lack of direct evidence to guide antiplatelet strategies in this setting. In this context, available evidence is largely derived from indirect data and observational studies. To contribute to this field, our research group conducted a prospective observational single-centre study from June 2021 to June 2024, including 443 patients with suspected NSTE-ACS undergoing CAG. Patients were monitored during their hospital stay for pretreatment-related bleeding events, ischaemic events and misdiagnosis, with 84.0% of the study group having antiplatelet pretreatment. Ischaemic events, bleeding events and cardiovascular mortality occurred in 5.0%, 4.1% and 1.8%, respectively. Ischaemic events were more frequent in the non-pretreatment group (10.3% versus 4.1%; p=0.030), whereas no differences were found in bleeding events between groups (1.4% versus 4.6%; p=0.216). MI before CAG (defined as a new ischaemic event during hospitalisation, re-MI in patients with NSTEMI or MI in patients with an initial diagnosis of UA) and type 4b MI rate were lower in the pretreatment group (1.6% versus 8.5%; p<0.001 and 0.3% versus 2.8%; p=0.016, respectively). After adjusting for covariates, pretreatment was associated with a lower incidence of ischaemic events (OR 0.35; 95% CI [0.135–0.928]; p=0.035), whereas it was not associated with bleeding events (OR 3.68; 95% CI [0.427–31.651]; p=0.236). In addition, a lower estimated glomerular filtration rate and active malignancy were associated with bleeding events, while chronic ischaemic heart disease was associated with ischaemic events in these patients. 22 These findings should be considered exploratory and used to generate hypotheses, and should not be used to inform clinical decision-making without confirmation from RCTs.

In summary, the decision to pretreat patients with NSTE-ACS should be individualised. Real-world practice may also involve treatment delays that are longer than those reported in RCTs, and pretreatment may have a role if the time to CAG is prolonged. 23 To support this process, we have identified different patient profiles: those who may benefit, those who may be harmed and situations in which pretreatment should be avoided: Patients who may benefit from pretreatment: those presenting with NSTE-ACS without diagnostic uncertainty in whom CAG is planned >24 hours.

Patients who may be harmed by pretreatment: those with suspected alternative diagnoses, such as acute aortic syndromes, pulmonary embolism or stroke, or who have a high bleeding risk. When to avoid pretreatment: patients in whom CAG is planned within <24 hours or who have a high likelihood of requiring cardiac surgery that could be delayed if pretreatment is administered. We developed an algorithm ( Figure 1 ) to help clinicians select those patients who may benefit from pretreatment administration, depending on CAG accessibility and other clinical features.

Discussion Clinical guidelines base pretreatment recommendations on the planned timing to undergo CAG, considering antiplatelet pretreatment when early CAG (performed within 24 hours of admission) is not available. 24 RCTs have shown a lack of benefit of pretreatment with a P2Y 12 inhibitor in reducing ischaemic events in patients presenting with ACS. 7 , 8 However, the time from P2Y 12 inhibitor loading dose to CAG was about 2 hours and 4.3 hours in the ISAR-REACT 5 and the ACCOAST trials, respectively. This does not give enough time to assess the hypothetical benefit of pretreatment in reducing ischaemic events and, furthermore, cannot be extrapolated to the usual clinical practice in centres that do not have rapid access to a cath lab. 7 , 8 The DUBIUS trial, with a median time to CAG of 23.3 hours, was prematurely interrupted, showing no differences in ischaemic events and bleeding events between the pretreatment group that was given ticagrelor and the non-pretreatment group. 21 In contrast, we found a reduction in the overall ischaemic events in patients who received pretreatment. We observed a significant decrease in the rate of stent thrombosis and a reduction in MI before CAG in the pretreatment group. 22

Regarding stent thrombosis, it is a rare but dramatic complication associated with MI and cardiac death. Stent thrombosis mechanisms are related to intracranial pressure techniques, such as stent malapposition and underexpansion. Some authors consider that prevention, including the use of pretreatment with a P2Y 12 inhibitor, is the only effective treatment for this severe form of coronary stent failure. 23 Our results, showing a significant reduction of stent thrombosis in the pretreatment group, support this hypothesis. Interestingly, the percentage of ischaemic events did not differ depending on whether CAG was delayed beyond 24 hours.

Moreover, we did not find a higher rate of bleeding events in the pretreatment group, except in patients in whom CAG was deferred more than 24 hours. Our results could be explained by the longer times between the diagnosis of NSTE-ACS and the performance of the CAG in our study, where the time from P2Y 12 inhibitor loading dose to CAG was over 24 hours in 64.8% of patients. This fact is that this is representative of daily clinical practice, not only in centres that have limited access to the cath lab, but also in many hospitals during weekends and non-working days. 22 In fact, in a recently published prospective NSTE-ACS Spanish registry where the pretreatment rate was 69.7%, only 37.8% of the patients had an early CAG, and there was a low level occurrence of cardiovascular and bleeding events. 25

The NSTE-ACS ESC clinical guidelines point out that routine pretreatment may delay CABG and may be deleterious for a relevant proportion of patients with diagnoses other than NSTE-ACS, such as acute aortic syndromes, pulmonary embolism or intracranial bleeds. 26 On the one hand, in our study, we registered only one case of acute aortic syndrome in the non-pretreatment group. Of note, all patients included in our registry were assessed by a cardiologist and a bedside echocardiogram was performed. This factor may explain our low rate of misdiagnosis of NSTE-ACS with other clinical conditions that may present with chest pain, in which pretreatment may be associated with severe complications. On the other hand, recent data from the RAPID CABG trial show that an early surgical strategy, 2–3 days after ticagrelor cessation, was non-inferior in incurring severe or massive bleeding compared to delaying surgery until 5–7 days. 18 In our study, all patients in whom CABG was planned remained stable, and none of them required emergency surgery. We found a median time from CAG to CABG of over 15 days. Surgery delay could not be attributed to the antiplatelet pretreatment but to the need for a pre-surgical study and approval by the reference surgical centre. This surgery delay could be explained by the lack of a local cardiac surgical team in our centre.

Current ACS ESC clinical guidelinesdo not differentiate between UA and NSTEMI in the antiplatelet treatment recommendations. 26 Since the era of high-sensitivity cTn, the proportion of patients classified with MI has increased, with a corresponding reduction in the diagnosis of UA. 27 Patients with UA generally present with a lower baseline ischaemic risk compared with those with MI. In this context, the effects of antiplatelet pretreatment may differ between these two clinical presentations; however, current evidence is insufficient to support differential treatment strategies. Adequately powered RCTs would be required to clarify whether such differences exist and whether they are clinically relevant.

In contrast to the ongoing controversy surrounding antiplatelet pretreatment, other pharmacological strategies in ACS have shown more consistent benefit when administered early. In particular, high-dose statin loading prior to PCI has been associated with a reduction in periprocedural myocardial injury and improved clinical outcomes. A meta-analysis by Borovac et al. demonstrated that early administration of high-dose atorvastatin or rosuvastatin in ACS patients undergoing PCI significantly reduced the incidence of periprocedural MI, with a favourable safety profile. 28 These findings suggest that, unlike antiplatelet pretreatment – where the balance between ischaemic and bleeding risk is highly dependent on context – statin pretreatment may provide more consistent benefit across different clinical scenarios. This contrast underscores the need for a tailored approach to pharmacological pretreatment strategies for patients with NSTE-ACS.

Background The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 0/1h‐high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs‐cTn)T/I‐algorithms have lower efficacy in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting. We hypothesized that in these high‐risk patients, the longer time to the second blood draw within the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms would increase efficacy, defined as the proportion of patients triaged to rule‐in/out of myocardial infarction, versus the ESC‐0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms.

Methods In a prospective international multicenter diagnostic study including patients presenting to the emergency department with acute chest discomfort, final diagnoses were centrally adjudicated according to the Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction. Safety and efficacy of the guideline‐recommended ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms using assay‐specific use‐optimized cut‐offs were directly compared in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting. Findings were externally validated in an independent prospective US multicenter study.

Results Among 356 patients (median [interquartile range] age 73 [64–80] years, prevalence of non–ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction [NSTEMI]: 31% [n=112]), sensitivity for rule‐out of NSTEMI was high for the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithms (0/1h: 100% [95% CI 96.7–100]; 0/2h: Sensitivity: 99.1% [95% CI 95.1–99.8]). Specificity for rule‐in of NSTEMI was also high (0/1h: 97.1% [95% CI 94.2–98.6]; 0/2h 98.4% [95% CI 95.9–99.4]). Efficacy was 50.6% for 0/1h and 58.4% for 0/2h (difference: 7.9% [95% CI 4.2–11.5]). Findings with higher efficacy for 0/2h versus 0/1h were confirmed using hs‐cTnI‐Architect (difference in efficacy 3.1% [95% CI 0.1–6.1]) and using hs‐cTnI‐Atellica in the external validation cohort (n=178; difference in efficacy 9% [95% CI 4.5–13.5]).

Conclusions The ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms have higher efficacy and comparable safety versus the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting. Registration URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique Identifier: NCT00470587 .

Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms ESC European Society of Cardiology hs‐cTn high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin hs‐cTnT/I high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin T/I NPV negative predictive value PPV positive predictive value Clinical Perspective What Is New?

In emergency department patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting presenting with acute chest discomfort, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 0/2h‐high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin T/I (hs‐cTnT/I)‐algorithms increased efficacy versus the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms by triaging an additional 3% to 9% of patients to definitive rule‐out or rule‐in while maintaining very high safety and accuracy for non–ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction. What Are the Clinical Implications?

Using the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting can modestly improve emergency department throughput by reducing the observe‐zone proportion without compromising rule‐out or rule‐in performance, but the workflow trade‐off of a longer sampling interval should be weighed against faster decision‐making with the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms. A pragmatic approach may be to apply the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms as the default strategy and obtain an additional 2‐hour sample for patients with coronary artery bypass grafting who remain in the observe zone to enable re‐triage using ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms cutoffs.

In patients with complex coronary artery disease, the preferred treatment option is coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). 1 , 2 It is the most commonly performed cardiac surgical procedure, and due to demographic aging and improvements in secondary prevention, the number of patients with prior CABG is steadily increasing. 3 , 4 Because of their advanced coronary artery disease and multiple comorbidities, patients with prior CABG presenting with acute chest discomfort to the emergency department (ED) are at particularly high risk of experiencing a myocardial infarction (MI). 5 , 6

It is therefore concerning that all 3 diagnostic pillars in the early diagnosis of MI, that is, chest pain characteristics, the 12‐lead ECG, and high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs‐cTn) T/I, have recently been shown to have lower diagnostic accuracy in patients with prior CABG. 5 , 7 , 8 While the safety of rule‐out and accuracy of rule‐in were maintained when applying the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms, their efficacy, defined as the proportion of patients triaged to either definite rule‐out or rule‐in of MI, was lower in patients with prior CABG compared with those without, resulting in prolonged length of stay in the ED and increased resource utilization. 5 ,

7 , 8 Consequently, there is a major unmet clinical need to further improve early triage of high‐risk patients with prior CABG. In a post‐hoc analysis of 2 large prospective cohorts, we therefore performed a direct paired comparison of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn algorithms, systematically quantifying differences in safety and efficacy and externally validating the findings, to test the hypothesis that extending the sampling interval to 2 hours may improve triage efficacy in patients with prior CABG by better differentiating frequent chronic hs‐cTn elevations from acute myocardial injury.

METHODS Study Design The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. This is a post hoc analysis from the APACE (Advantageous Predictors of Acute Coronary Syndromes Evaluation) study, enrolling consecutive adult patients presenting to the ED with acute chest discomfort ( ClinicalTrials.gov registry, number NCT00470587 ). 5 , 9

The central adjudication of the final diagnoses was performed by 2 independent cardiologists twice: once including serial measurements of hs‐cTnT (Elecsys, Roche Diagnostics) and once using hs‐cTnI (ARCHITECT STAT, Abbott Laboratories) in addition to all available clinical information including cardiac imaging, the local (hs)‐cTnT/I measurements, and study‐specific assessments including prospective assessment of 34 chest pain/discomfort characteristics and clinical follow‐up up to 90 days according to current guidelines and the fourth universal definition of MI. 10 , 11

To minimize a potential bias when directly comparing the performance of hs‐cTnT and hs‐cTnI based early triage algorithms in patients where the adjudicated diagnosis was either based on hs‐cTnT or hs‐cTnI, 2 independent adjudications were done to balance the effect of possibly diverging results for hs‐cTnT versus hs‐cTnI in favor of the hs‐cTn assay included in the central adjudication. 12 , 13 , 14

As the aim of the study was a direct comparison of the performance of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in the same patients with prior CABG surgery, only patients with prior CABG and available hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys (analysis 1) and hs‐cTnI‐Architect (analysis 2) concentrations at presentation (0h), 1h and 2h were included. The 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes recommend excluding ST‐segment–elevation MI (STEMI) before applying the 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn algorithms to rule‐out/in non–ST‐segment–elevation MI (NSTEMI). 10

We have therefore excluded patients with STEMI for this analysis. Furthermore, we excluded patients in whom the final diagnosis remained unclear (“unknown diagnosis”) even after central adjudication and in whom hs‐cTn concentrations were elevated, thereby possibly indicating MI. This small group of patients with cardiomyocyte injury reflects clinical reality where the reliable diagnosis or exclusion of MI is not feasible because of insufficient clinical work‐up and information. These patients were also excluded from all previous diagnostic analyses in the APACE trial (Figure 1 ). 7 , 8 , 15

Figure 1 Flowchart. Analysis 1 and Analysis 2. CABG indicates coronary artery bypass grafting; and hs‐cTn, high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin. Blood samples were collected at ED presentation (0 hour) and at 1, 2, 3, and 6 hours after presentation. Serial sampling was discontinued if patients were discharged from the ED or transferred to another unit. Measurements were performed in plasma samples immediately centrifuged and then frozen for later measurements in a core laboratory. Analytical details of hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys and hs‐cTnI‐Architect have been described elsewhere. 16 Samples for the 1h and 2h concentrations were obtained at median 60 (IQR 55–70) and 120 (IQR 116–131) minutes, respectively.

Reporting is in accordance with the STARD statement (Table S1 ) and adheres to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was obtained from local ethics committees, and all participants provided written informed consent. External Cohort Results were externally validated in the HIGH‐US using 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Atellica‐algorithms. The methodology of the HIGH‐US study has been described in detail before. 17

In brief, adults aged 22 years and older who presented to the ED with any suspected acute MI prompting the clinical ordering of a cardiac troponin level test and who signed consent were prospectively enrolled in a Food and Drug Administration 510(k) study. The EDs were located in 29 centers across the United States in both tertiary urban settings and community hospitals. The adjudication panel consisted of cardiologists and emergency physicians, with 5 physicians (at least 2 members of each specialty) assigned to each case. These individuals and the treating emergency physicians were blinded to the hs‐cTnI results. Adjudicators determined acute MI diagnosis (both type 1 and type 2) with the Universal Definition of MI. Final diagnosis was determined by the majority adjudicator opinion.

17 Blood samples were scheduled at presentation (0h), after 1h (median time 57 minutes) and after 2.5h (median time 141 minutes) and the hs‐cTnI‐Atellica immunoassay (Siemens) was used. 8 , 17 Outcome The diagnostic outcome was an adjudicated diagnosis of index NSTEMI (type 1 or type 2). The prognostic outcome was all‐cause death at 30 and 730 days.

Objectives Primary objective was the direct comparison of the efficacy, defined as the proportion of patients triaged to definite rule‐out or rule‐in of MI by the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms using hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys and hs‐cTnI‐Architect in patients with prior CABG. Secondary objective included comparison of the safety (defined as negative predictive value [NPV] and sensitivity) for rule‐out NSTEMI and accuracy (defined as positive predictive value [PPV] and specificity) for rule‐in NSTEMI as well as long‐term survival according to the classification of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms.
Statistical Analysis The ESC 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms were applied using assay‐specific use‐optimized cut‐offs as recommended in current guidelines (Table 1 ). 18

We performed the analysis of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithms (analysis 1) based on the adjudication including serial hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys measurements as part of the study specific data set. The performance of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Architect‐algorithms (analysis 2) was based on a second independent adjudication including serial hs‐cTnI‐Architect (rather than hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys) measurements from the study samples as part of the study specific data set. NPV/sensitivity and PPV/specificity were derived from contingency tables comparing the algorithm‐based triage classification (rule‐out/observe/rule‐in) with the adjudicated index diagnosis of NSTEMI using the Wilson score method without continuity correction.

19 As NPV and PPV are prevalence‐dependent, we therefore also report sensitivity and specificity. Comparison of the efficacy, defined as the proportion of all patients triaged to definite rule‐out or rule‐in of MI, was calculated using the McNemar test. 20 Furthermore, we performed exploratory sensitivity analyses including type 1 MI only, in patients with renal dysfunction (defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 ) and in the elderly (≥70 years). 21 , 22 Table 1 Assay‐Specific Cutoffs for the European Society of Cardiology 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐Algorithms 0/1h‐algorithm Rule‐out Rule‐in Very low *

Low No 1h delta High 1h delta hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys <5 <12 <3 ≥52 ≥5 hs‐cTnI‐Architect <4 <5 <2 ≥64 ≥6 hs‐cTnI‐Atellica <3 <6 <3 ≥120 ≥12 0/2h‐algorithm Rule‐out Rule‐in Very low * Low No 2h delta High 2h delta hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys <5 <14 <4 ≥52 ≥10 hs‐cTnI‐Architect <4 <6 <2 ≥64 ≥15 hs‐cTnI‐Atellica <3 <8 <7 ≥120 ≥20 hs‐cTn, high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin. * If chest pain onset >3 hours.

To provide clinically meaningful short‐ and long‐term prognosis and to enable comparability with prior studies reporting prognostic outcomes after application of ESC hs‐cTn algorithms, survival at 30 days and 730 days of follow‐up according to the classification provided by the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐ hs‐cTn‐algorithms was plotted in Kaplan–Meier curves and the log‐rank test was used to assess differences in survival between groups without multivariable analyses. 23 , 24

Patients lost to follow‐up or alive at day 730 were right‐censored. Hazard ratios for all‐cause mortality at 730 days were estimated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models with rule‐out as the reference category, adjusting for age, sex and estimated glomerular filtration rate.

RESULTS Demographic Data Overall, 356 patients (median [Interquartile range, IQR] age 73 [64.0‐80.0] years, 15% [n=54] women) were included in the analysis of the 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithms. The prevalence of NSTEMI was 31% (n=112, Table 2 and Table S2 ). For the analysis of the 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Architect‐algorithms, 352 patients (median [IQR] age 73.0 [64.0, 80.0] years, 15% [n=53] women) with 104/352 (30%) having an NSTEMI were eligible. External validation in the HIGH‐US cohort showed similar results (Figure S2A and S2B ). Over 730 days, patients classified to the rule‐in zone using the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT‐algorithm had a significantly higher adjusted risk of all‐cause mortality compared with the rule‐out group (HR 4.13, 95% CI 1.29–13.19), whereas no significant difference was observed for the observe zone (HR 1.58, 95% CI 0.50–5.00). Similar results were seen for the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐algorithm as well as for the ESC 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐algorithms.

DISCUSSION This study tested the hypothesis that in patients with prior CABG, who are at increased risk of MI when presenting with acute chest discomfort to the ED, and in whom the current standard‐of‐care ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms demonstrate reduced efficacy, the longer interval to the 2nd blood draw within the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms (2h versus 1h) would improve efficacy, defined as the proportion of patients triaged to definite rule‐out or rule‐in of MI, when compared with the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms. We report 4 major findings.
First, all ESC 0/1‐ and 0/2h‐algorithms had a very high safety, as quantified by NPV and sensitivity for rule‐out of NSTEMI, and high accuracy, as quantified by PPV and specificity for rule‐in.

Second, in direct comparison with the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms, the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms significantly improved efficacy, triaging a higher proportion of patients to either rule‐out or rule‐in. This was consistent across hs‐cTnT/I assays used and confirmed in the independent external validation cohort. Third, the magnitude of this increase in efficacy was clinically meaningful, ranging from 3.1% to 9%. Fourth, cumulative 30‐ and 730‐day all‐cause mortality for both assays and algorithms were highest in patients triaged to the rule‐in group, lowest in the rule‐out group, and intermediate in the observe zone. Risk stratification was comparable for the ESC 0/1‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms.

These findings extend and corroborate previous studies focusing on patients with prior CABG and documenting (1) the high incidence of MI and unstable angina, (2) the lower diagnostic accuracy of chest pain characteristics, ECG, and hs‐cTn, and (3) the resulting lower efficacy of the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithm and prolonged ED stay. 5 , 7 As a consequence of these observations, prior studies have advocated for liberal use of coronary angiography in both the rule‐in as well as the observe zone to maximize early revascularization opportunities. 5 , 8

Our findings suggest that using the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in patients with prior CABG may be preferable. Clinically, compared with the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms, use of the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms translates into an absolute throughput benefit of approximately 3 to 9 additional CABG patients per 100 being definitively triaged. However, 2 arguments may favor continued use of the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in patients with CABG. First, clinical decision‐making is faster with 0/1h versus 0/2h in patients where the initial 0h concentration does not permit immediate triage. Second, applying the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms as the default strategy and switching to the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in patients with prior CABG may complicate ED workflows and possibly increase the risk of human error. However, as clear strategies for patients triaged to the observe‐zone remain scarce and derived cutoffs only exist for hs‐cTnT, a possible strategy might involve using the ESC 0/1h hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms, and if patients with prior CABG remain in the observe zone, a blood draw after 2 hours could be performed, using the cutoffs of the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms for triage (Figure S3 ).

15 The likely reason for the higher efficacy of the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms is the longer sampling interval (2 h instead of 1 h), which facilitated the reliable differentiation of MI with its acute rise and fall in hs‐cTnT/I from chronic cardiomyocyte injury, which is particularly common in patients with prior CABG. It is plausible that the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms could also have higher efficacy versus the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in other patient populations with a high prevalence of chronic cardiomyocyte injury such as the elderly and patients with renal dysfunction. Further studies are warranted to test this hypothesis.

Beyond the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms, 2 other strategies might help to overcome current unmet needs in the diagnostic work‐up of patients with prior CABG presenting with acute chest discomfort to the ED: (1) dedicated triage algorithms developed for patients remaining in the observe zone 15 ; (2) advanced machine learning models that integrate hs‐cTn concentration together with ECG and clinical features. 25 , 26 , 27 , 28

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, although a very sophisticated methodology was used to centrally adjudicate the final diagnoses, some patients may have been misclassified. Second, results may not be generalized to patients with endstage renal disease requiring dialysis. Third, as this is a post hoc analysis, no a priori sample size calculation was performed. Although this represents one of the largest CABG‐specific diagnostic data sets to date and, to our knowledge, the largest analysis providing a direct paired comparison of the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithm and the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithm in patients with prior CABG, statistical power may still be limited for certain subgroup comparisons. Fourth, the median sampling time for the 2‐hour samples in the external validation cohort was 141 minutes, which may have led to a small overestimation of efficacy. Fifth, these findings are limited to the use of hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys, hs‐cTnI‐Architect and hs‐cTnI‐Atellica as the guidelines recommend assay‐specific cutoffs for all the respective hs‐cTnT/I assays. Sixth, the prevalence of NSTEMI differed between the APACE cohort and the external cohort (HIGH‐US), which limits direct comparisons of prevalence‐dependent metrics such as PPV and NPV across cohorts; accordingly, these measures should be interpreted within each cohort. Seventh, Kaplan–Meier analyses were unadjusted and descriptive; thus, they should be interpreted cautiously and not as evidence of causal effects of one ESC‐hs‐cTn‐algorithm over the other.
CONCLUSIONS Our findings suggest that the 0/2h‐algorithm may modestly increase efficacy, though further confirmatory studies are needed before considering potential changes to clinical practice.

CONTEXT: Women are generally older than men at hospitalization for myocardial infarction (MI) and also present less frequently with chest pain/discomfort. However, few studies have taken age into account when examining sex differences in clinical presentation and mortality. OBJECTIVE: To examine the relationship between sex and symptom presentation and between sex, symptom presentation, and hospital mortality, before and after accounting for age in patients hospitalized with MI. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PATIENTS: Observational study from the National Registry of Myocardial Infarction, 1994-2006, of 1,143,513 registry patients (481,581 women and 661,932 men).

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: We examined predictors of MI presentation without chest pain and the relationship between age, sex, and hospital mortality. RESULTS: The proportion of MI patients who presented without chest pain was significantly higher for women than men (42.0% [95% CI, 41.8%-42.1%] vs 30.7% [95% CI, 30.6%-30.8%]; P < .001). There was a significant interaction between age and sex with chest pain at presentation, with a larger sex difference in younger than older patients, which became attenuated with advancing age.

Multivariable adjusted age-specific odds ratios (ORs) for lack of chest pain for women (referent, men) were younger than 45 years, 1.30 (95% CI, 1.23-1.36); 45 to 54 years, 1.26 (95% CI, 1.22-1.30); 55 to 64 years, 1.24 (95% CI, 1.21-1.27); 65 to 74 years, 1.13 (95% CI, 1.11-1.15); and 75 years or older, 1.03 (95% CI,

1.02-1.04). Two-way interaction (sex and age) on MI presentation without chest pain was significant (P < .001). The in-hospital mortality rate was 14.6% for women and 10.3% for men. Younger women presenting without chest pain had greater hospital mortality than younger men without chest pain, and these sex differences decreased or even reversed with advancing age, with adjusted OR for age younger than 45 years, 1.18 (95% CI, 1.00-1.39); 45 to 54 years, 1.13 (95%

CI, 1.02-1.26); 55 to 64 years, 1.02 (95% CI, 0.96-1.09); 65 to 74 years, 0.91 (95% CI, 0.88-0.95); and 75 years or older, 0.81 (95% CI, 0.79-0.83). The 3-way interaction (sex, age, and chest pain) on mortality was significant (P < .001). CONCLUSION: In this registry of patients hospitalized with MI, women were more likely than men to present without chest pain and had higher mortality than men within the same age group, but sex differences in clinical presentation without chest pain and in mortality were attenuated with increasing age. When faced with a patient with acute chest pain, clinicians must distinguish myocardial infarction (MI) from all other causes of acute chest pain. If MI is suspected, current therapeutic practice includes deciding whether to administer thrombolysis or primary percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty and whether to admit patients to a coronary care unit. The former decision is based on electrocardiographic (ECG) changes, including ST-segment elevation or left bundle-branch block, the latter on the likelihood of the patient's having unstable high-risk ischemia or MI without ECG changes. Despite advances in investigative modalities, a focused history and physical examination followed by an ECG remain the key tools for the diagnosis of MI. The most powerful features that increase the probability of MI, and their associated likelihood ratios (LRs), are new ST-segment elevation (LR range, 5.7-53.9); new Q wave (LR range,

5.3-24.8); chest pain radiating to both the left and right arm simultaneously (LR, 7.1); presence of a third heart sound (LR, 3.2); and hypotension (LR, 3.1). The most powerful features that decrease the probability of MI are a normal ECG result (LR range, 0.1-0.3), pleuritic chest pain (LR, 0.2), chest pain reproduced by palpation (LR range, 0.2-0.4), sharp or stabbing chest pain (LR, 0.3), and positional chest pain (LR, 0.3). Computer-derived algorithms that depend on clinical examination and ECG findings might improve the classification of patients according to the probability that an MI is causing their chest pain. CONTEXT: The chest pain history, physical examination, determination of coronary artery disease (CAD) risk factors, and the initial electrocardiogram compose the information immediately available to clinicians to help determine the probability of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) or acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients with chest pain. However, conflicting data exist about the usefulness of the chest pain history and which components are most useful. OBJECTIVE: To identify the elements of the chest pain history that may be most helpful to the clinician in identifying ACS in patients presenting with chest pain.

EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: MEDLINE and Ovid were searched from 1970 to September 2005 by using specific key words and Medical Subject Heading terms. Reference lists of these articles and current cardiology textbooks were also consulted. EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS: Certain chest pain characteristics decrease the likelihood of ACS or AMI, namely, pain that is stabbing, pleuritic, positional, or reproducible by palpation (likelihood ratios [LRs] 0.2-0.3). Conversely, chest pain that radiates to one shoulder or both shoulders or arms or is precipitated by exertion is associated with LRs (2.3-4.7) that increase the likelihood of

ACS. The chest pain history itself has not proven to be a powerful enough predictive tool to obviate the need for at least some diagnostic testing. Combinations of elements of the chest pain history with other initially available information, such as a history of CAD, have identified certain groups that may be safe for discharge without further evaluation, but further study is needed before such a recommendation can be considered reasonable.

CONCLUSION: Although certain elements of the chest pain history are associated with increased or decreased likelihoods of a diagnosis of ACS or AMI, none of them alone or in combination identify a group of patients that can be safely discharged without further diagnostic testing. BACKGROUND: The focus of the diagnostic process in chest pain patients at the emergency department is to identify both low and high risk patients for an acute coronary syndrome (ACS). The HEART score was designed to facilitate this process. This study is a prospective validation of the HEART score. METHODS: A total of 2440 unselected patients presented with chest pain at the cardiac emergency department of ten participating hospitals in The Netherlands.

The HEART score was assessed as soon as the first lab results and ECG were obtained. Primary endpoint was the occurrence of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) within 6 weeks. Secondary endpoints were (i) the occurrence of AMI and death, (ii) ACS and (iii) the performance of a coronary angiogram. The performance of the HEART score was compared with the TIMI and GRACE scores. RESULTS: Low HEART scores (values 0-3) were calculated in 36.4% of the patients. MACE occurred in 1.7%. In patients with HEART scores 4-6, MACE was diagnosed in 16.6%. In patients with high HEART scores (values 7-10), MACE occurred in 50.1%.

The c-statistic of the HEART score (0.83) is significantly higher than the c-statistic of TIMI (0.75)and GRACE (0.70) respectively (p 98% certainty.
